title: Recovering the Lost Art of Hospitality
subtitle: On the open table as ministry, biblical hospitality to the stranger, and how the church recovers a practice it has handed off to restaurants

sections.title: A Command We Turned Into a Hobby
sections.body:
Hospitality has become a magazine word. We think of matching napkins and a clean guest room and a host who entertains people who could return the favor. That is not what the Bible means, and the gap is not small.

The word in the New Testament is philoxenia. Love of the stranger.

Not love of the guest who will love you back. Love of the one who cannot repay you, the one you do not yet know, the one the world has no reason to feed. We took a command and shrank it into a personality trait that some people happen to have and others happily skip. But the Scriptures do not offer hospitality as a gift for the extroverted few. They command it of all of us, plainly, repeatedly, and they tie it to nothing less than whether we have understood the gospel that took us in when we were strangers. We were the outsider once. Hospitality is just the memory of that, turned into a meal.

sections.title: Jesus Did Most of His Work at a Table
sections.body:
Read the Gospels and watch where Jesus keeps showing up. At dinner. Eating with tax collectors. Eating with Pharisees. Eating with sinners until it became the charge against him. This man eats with sinners.

They meant it as an accusation. It turned out to be the whole point.

So much of his ministry happened over food that his enemies could summarize him by his table. He fed the five thousand. He cooked breakfast on a beach for the men who had abandoned him. He made the central act of Christian worship a meal. The early church spread not mainly through stadiums but through homes, through shared tables, through the strange sight of slaves and masters and Jews and Gentiles eating as equals in a world that kept everyone in their place. The table was where the gospel became visible. It still is. A church can preach welcome from the platform every Sunday and remain a fortress, because welcome is not a slogan. It is a chair pulled out and a plate set down.

sections.title: An Open Door Costs Something
sections.body:
We do not practice hospitality because it is expensive, and we should be honest that it is. It costs time we do not have, money we are saving, and the loss of the evening we wanted to ourselves.

Hospitality is the deliberate decision to let other people into your actual life, mess and all.

That is why we hide behind the excuse that the house is not ready, the meal is not impressive, the schedule is full. None of it is the real reason. The real reason is that we have built lives sealed off from interruption and called the sealing off rest. But the open table requires a kind of dying, a willingness to be inconvenienced, exposed, and tired for the sake of someone who walked in lonely. The host who waits for the perfect house will never open the door. So open it imperfectly. Feed people from a kitchen that is not clean enough, at a table that does not match, with food that is plain. The stranger did not come for the décor. He came to be let in. Let him in.

sections.title: Invite the Ones Who Cannot Repay
sections.body:
Jesus gave one of his sharpest instructions about a dinner party, and almost no one obeys it. When you give a feast, he said, do not invite your friends and your rich neighbors who will invite you back. Invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind.

Invite the ones who cannot return the favor. That is the test that exposes us.

Most of our hospitality is really an exchange, a trading of dinners among people who keep careful unspoken accounts. The gospel kind keeps no account. It seeks out the new family no one has welcomed, the widow who eats every meal alone, the international student who has not been inside a home all year, the awkward man no group has absorbed, the single person the married couples forgot. These are the guests of the kingdom, and the church that fills its tables with them looks like heaven and the church that fills its tables only with its friends looks like everywhere else. Make your guest list from the people who can do nothing for you. That is the list Jesus would have written, and he said as much.

sections.title: We Outsourced the Table and Lost Something
sections.body:
We handed our hospitality to the professionals. The restaurant feeds the stranger now. The agency houses him. The app delivers his meal. And we told ourselves this was progress while a generation grew up lonelier than any before it, surrounded by screens and starved of a table.

I have let people sit alone whom I could have invited, because my evening was mine and I wanted to keep it.

The church cannot fix loneliness with a better program. Loneliness is healed at a table or it is not healed at all, by people who decide that another human being is worth an evening of their one short life. So set a table this week and put someone at it who has no claim on you. Do it again next week. Build the muscle the culture let atrophy. We will not argue people into the kingdom while we keep our doors locked against them. But a person who has been fed at your table, seen at your table, known at your table, has tasted something the world cannot give and may begin to wonder where it came from. It came from a Lord who set a table for us while we were still strangers. The least we can do is set one for someone else.
